---
title: "Accessible interactive SVG map"
author: "Pascal Cauhepe"
author_bio: "Web developer for 15 years, now focused on digital accessibility: RGAA audits, accessible components, and tools. Based near Toulouse, France, and currently looking for my next role."
date: 2026-12-13
author_links:
  - label: "Site"
    url: "https://p11e.dev/"
    link_label: "Website"
intro: "<p>SVG maps: can you make them accessible? How far can we go?</p>"
image: "advent26_1"
active: true
---

On many sites, maps are added without any thought for accessibility: countries you can click but cannot reach with the keyboard, links without a name, colour as the only way to tell one area from another.
When accessibility is taken into account, the map itself often stays as it is, and an alternative is added next to it: a table, a list, a text description. It is a reasonable approach, and it gives access to the data. But the alternative does not always carry the map's point of view: a table sorted alphabetically, for example, loses the groups and the contrasts the map was designed to show.
Maybe there is something in between. An SVG map is code, after all: like HTML, it can carry roles, links and names. Can the map itself become accessible, and keep its point of view? And how far can we go?

Let's explore.

## Part 1: a map of links

My first idea was a map of police violence against young people in France, but it would have needed far too many links for a demo. Instead, I made an SVG map that links to the articles published in this calendar over the past few days.
To keep things “simple”, I only show articles by European authors (my apologies to the authors outside Europe), and when a country has several authors, I link to the earliest article.

  </ul>
 </div>
 <script type="module">
  // Refits a tooltip's frame when a user tool makes its text larger.
  const fitTooltips = (map) => {
    const PAD = { x: 1.5, edge: 0.5 };
    const view = map.viewBox.baseVal;
    const given = new Map();
    const fit = (tooltip) => {
      const frame = tooltip.querySelector('.tm-tooltip-frame');
      const label = tooltip.querySelector('.tm-tooltip-text');
      const [first, ...others] = label.querySelectorAll('tspan');
      if (!given.has(tooltip)) {
        given.set(tooltip, {
          ...Object.fromEntries(['x', 'y', 'width', 'height'].map((key) => [key, frame[key].baseVal.value])),
          baseline: first.y.baseVal[0].value,
        });
      }
      const start = given.get(tooltip);
      const style = getComputedStyle(label);
      const size = parseFloat(style.fontSize);
      const step = Math.max(1.2 * size, parseFloat(style.lineHeight) || 0);
      others.forEach((line) => line.setAttribute('dy', step));
      // The same proportions as tooltip-layout.js: 6 units of height for a 4-unit font.
      const width = label.getBBox().width + PAD.x * 2;
      const height = 1.5 * size + others.length * step;
      const fits = width <= start.width && height <= start.height;
      const box = fits ? start : {
        width: Math.max(width, start.width),
        height: Math.max(height, start.height),
      };
      if (!fits) {
        // The bottom edge stays, close to the country (and to the Belgian and Dutch bridges);
        // the frame grows upwards and on both sides, inside the map.
        box.y = Math.max(start.y + start.height - box.height, view.y + PAD.edge);
        box.x = Math.min(Math.max(start.x + start.width / 2 - box.width / 2, view.x + PAD.edge),
          view.x + view.width - PAD.edge - box.width);
      }
      for (const key of ['x', 'y', 'width', 'height']) frame.setAttribute(key, box[key]);
      for (const line of [first, ...others]) line.setAttribute('x', box.x + box.width / 2);
      first.setAttribute('y', fits ? start.baseline : box.y + 1.02 * size);
    };
    const observer = new ResizeObserver((entries) => {
      for (const { target, contentRect } of entries) {
        if (contentRect.width > 0) fit(target.closest('.tm-tooltip'));
      }
    });
    for (const label of map.querySelectorAll('.tm-tooltip-text')) observer.observe(label);
    map.classList.add('is-fitted');
    return observer;
  };
  // Escape hides the shown tooltip (WCAG 1.4.13, dismissible), as in tooltips.js. Showing it
  // is left to CSS; the script only adds .is-dismissed to the map, and removes it when the
  // pointer moves to another link or the focus does.
  customElements.define('advent-map', class extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
      const map = this.querySelector('.tm-advent');
      this.observer = fitTooltips(map);
      let pointed = null; // link under the pointer
      this.controller = new AbortController();
      const { signal } = this.controller;
      document.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
        if (event.key === 'Escape') map.classList.add('is-dismissed');
      }, { signal });
      map.addEventListener('pointerover', (event) => {
        const link = event.target.closest('a');
        if (link === pointed) return;
        pointed = link;
        map.classList.remove('is-dismissed');
      }, { signal });
      map.addEventListener('pointerleave', () => {
        pointed = null;
        map.classList.remove('is-dismissed');
      }, { signal });
      map.addEventListener('focusin', () => map.classList.remove('is-dismissed'), { signal });
    }
    disconnectedCallback() {
      this.controller.abort();
      this.observer.disconnect();
    }
  });
 </script>
</advent-map>


### Testing

#### With a mouse

Mouse users can hover a country to read its tooltip, then click it to open the article.

#### With a keyboard

Keyboard users can move from one country to the next with <kbd>Tab</kbd>: the tooltip shows on focus, and <kbd>Enter</kbd> opens the article.

#### With a screen reader

Because the `<svg>` and `<g>` elements carry the roles `list` and `listitem`, the accessibility tree is the same as for a list of links built with `<ul>` and `<li>`. Screen reader users can jump to the list (<kbd>L</kbd> with NVDA or JAWS), and find the links in the rotor (VoiceOver) or in the Elements List (NVDA).
The link to the article you are reading is announced as the current page, thanks to the `aria-current` attribute.

#### With voice control

What users see on each link is the number of the day: 1, 3, 10… The accessible names start with “Day 1”, then give the author's first name and their country. It might seem better to draw “Day 1” on the map, so that users of some assistive technologies could say “Click Day 1”. I tried, but it created other problems: there is not much room in Western Europe, and the longer labels overlapped each other and their neighbours. 
I am not a regular user of these tools, but the most comfortable way to use the map seems to be the grid, or key commands (“Tab”, “Enter”).

#### Colours

The links are not identified by their colour alone: they have a dot pattern, which changes to another pattern on `:hover` and `:focus-visible`.

#### Zoom and screen magnifiers

Depending on the level of zoom a user needs, the text of the tooltips can be hard to read.
As for WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.13 (Content on Hover or Focus), the tooltips are dismissible, with the <kbd>Escape</kbd> key, and hoverable. For Belgium (10) and the Netherlands (3), though, the tooltip is not right next to the country: an invisible “bridge” links them (the reason is explained below), and a user whose pointer leaves that bridge on the way will close the tooltip.
The native SVG `<title>` element would have been an alternative, since tooltips drawn by the browser fall under an exception of 1.4.13. I chose my own tooltips so that keyboard users can see them too.

### How it works

**A list of links.** The SVG has `role="list"`, and each country is a list item that contains a link.
The day numbers and the tooltips sit inside the `<a>`, so that hovering them keeps the link hovered.

```html
<svg role="list" viewBox="…">
  <g class="tm-context" aria-hidden="true">…</g>
  <g data-code="BE" role="listitem">
   <a href="/adventcalendar/2026/10/" aria-label="Day 10 by Michaël from Belgium">
    <path aria-hidden="true" data-piece="0" d="…"/>
    <g class="tm-day" aria-hidden="true">
     <line …/>
     <circle …/>
     <circle …/>
     <text …>10</text>
    </g>
    <rect aria-hidden="true" class="tm-bridge" …/>
    <g class="tm-tooltip" data-tooltip="BE" aria-hidden="true">
     <rect …/>
     <text …><tspan …>Day 10 by Michaël</tspan><tspan …>from Belgium</tspan></text>
    </g>
   </a>
  </g>
  <g role="listitem">
    <a href="/adventcalendar/2026/12/" aria-label="Day 12 by Krisztina Závecz from Hungary">
      <path aria-hidden="true" d="…"/>
      <g class="tm-day" aria-hidden="true">
        <circle …/><text …>12</text>
      </g>
      <g class="tm-tooltip" data-tooltip="HU" aria-hidden="true">
        <rect …/>
        <text …><tspan …>Day 12 by Krisztina</tspan><tspan …">from Hungary</tspan></text>
      </g>
    </a>
  </g>
</svg>
```


- The other countries are only decoration, hidden with `aria-hidden="true"`.
- The `<pattern>` elements, and the `<rect>` or `<path>` used for the bridges, need `aria-hidden="true"`; otherwise VoiceOver announces “image”.
- The countries whose article is not published yet are hidden too, and drawn with a “?” pattern.
- The current article has `aria-current="page"`. The CSS relies on that same attribute to style it, so that what you see and what you hear are less likely to drift apart.

**Patterns, not only colours.** 

```css
.tm-advent [role="listitem"] path { fill: url(#icon-dots); }

.tm-advent a:hover path,
.tm-advent a:focus-visible path { fill: url(#icon-hand); }
```

**Tooltips, not `<title>`.** A `<title>` inside the link would give it both a name and a native tooltip, but that tooltip does not show on keyboard focus in current browsers. So the name comes from `aria-label`, and my own tooltip, hidden from screen readers, serves both mouse and keyboard users. A few lines of JavaScript add the <kbd>Escape</kbd> key; showing and hiding the tooltip is left to CSS, with `:hover` and `:focus-visible`.
As mentioned above, `<title>` would have met WCAG Success Criterion 1.4.13 through its exception: <cite>The visual presentation of the additional content is controlled by the user agent</cite>. Keeping my own tooltips for keyboard users, however, runs into a limitation of SVG.
In SVG, elements are painted in DOM order: each one is drawn on top of the ones before it, and there is no `z-index` (SVG 2 planned one, but no browser implements it). A tooltip inside a country's `<a>` can therefore be covered by the countries that come after it in the DOM. Hence the careful placement of each tooltip, and the bridges between some countries and their tooltips: it works, but it is not perfect, and it requires some care whenever the map changes.

### Conclusion

With voice control or a screen magnifier, the experience can still be uncomfortable. This is partly due to my example: in the more common use case, the tooltips would only show country names, which are shorter, so the tooltips would be smaller, and the names easier to say with voice control (provided you know your geography).

Can we do without an alternative, then? Probably not. The map works for many users, but a plain HTML list of links remains the “safer” option, and nothing prevents us from adding one next to the map.




## Part 2: a choropleth map, two approaches

A choropleth map shows a value for each area, here each country, by grouping the values into classes and giving each class its own colour. It is one of the most common kinds of data maps, and it raises its own accessibility challenges: the information is carried first by colour, some areas are tiny, and the map is meant to be compared at a glance. Here, what matters is less each value than the groups the countries fall into.

The data comes from the EU statistics on income and living conditions (EU-SILC), published by Eurostat.
In 2025, 24.2% of people aged 16 or over in the EU reported some or severe long-standing limitations in their usual activities due to health problems.

> All of the indicators [&hellip;] are derived from self-reported data, so they are, to a certain extent, affected by respondents’ subjective perception as well as by their social and cultural background.
> Eurostat, [Population with disability](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Population_with_disability)

The 27 countries of the EU fall into five classes: under 20%, 20 to 25%, 25 to 30%, and 30% or more plus a class of its own for Luxembourg, which has no data for 2025. Each class has a pattern as well as a colour, so that it can be told apart without relying on colour alone. The other European countries are drawn in grey, as context.

### First attempt: the map at the centre

Move to a class with <kbd>Tab</kbd> and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>, or hover a country and click it.

 <script type="module">
  // Each class opens its dialog, as in class-dialogs.js. Escape hides the tooltips of the
  // hovered or focused class (WCAG 1.4.13, dismissible), as in class-tooltips.js: showing
  // them is left to CSS; the script only adds .is-dismissed to the map, and removes it when
  // the pointer moves to another class or the focus does.
  customElements.define('choropleth-classic', class extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
      const map = this.querySelector('.tm-1tw10');
      this.controller = new AbortController();
      const { signal } = this.controller;
      for (const button of map.querySelectorAll('.tm-class[role="button"]')) {
        const dialog = this.querySelector(`#tm-1tw10-dialog-${button.dataset.class}`);
        button.addEventListener('click', () => dialog.showModal(), { signal });
        // As on a native button: Enter acts on keydown, Space on keyup. Opening on Space's
        // keydown would let its keyup land on the dialog's Close button, and close it at once.
        button.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
          if (event.key === ' ') event.preventDefault(); // Space would scroll the page
          if (event.key === 'Enter') dialog.showModal();
        }, { signal });
        button.addEventListener('keyup', (event) => {
          if (event.key === ' ') dialog.showModal();
        }, { signal });
      }
      let pointed = null; // class under the pointer
      document.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
        if (event.key === 'Escape') map.classList.add('is-dismissed');
      }, { signal });
      map.addEventListener('pointerover', (event) => {
        const group = event.target.closest('.tm-class');
        if (group === pointed) return;
        pointed = group;
        map.classList.remove('is-dismissed');
      }, { signal });
      map.addEventListener('pointerleave', () => {
        pointed = null;
        map.classList.remove('is-dismissed');
      }, { signal });
      map.addEventListener('focusin', () => map.classList.remove('is-dismissed'), { signal });
    }
    disconnectedCallback() {
      this.controller.abort();
    }
  });
 </script>
</choropleth-classic>

To avoid a long series of tab stops, one per country, each class of the map is a single button, which opens a dialog listing its countries.
On hover or focus, the whole class is highlighted, and every country of the class shows its value; <kbd>Escape</kbd> hides these values, as on the map of links.


#### How it works

<g class="tm-class" role="button" tabindex="0" aria-haspopup="dialog"
   aria-label="20 to 25%, 10 countries">
  …countries of this class…
</g>
```

A `<g>` with `role="button"` is not a real button: a script has to provide what a `<button>` does natively, namely:

- opening the dialog on click;
- reacting to the <kbd>Enter</kbd> key and to the <kbd>Space</kbd> key.

#### What the tests say

It works with the keyboard, and screen readers announce the buttons, along with the fact that they open a dialog.
Without JavaScript, however, the buttons do nothing, the dialogs cannot be reached, and screen reader users have no access to the data at all.
Mouse users may be surprised to see the values of the whole class, when they only hovered one country.

With voice control, the map is hard to use. The classes are `<g>` elements grouping several countries; they are large, so the numbers or labels shown by voice control end up in seemingly random places.

With zoom or a screen magnifier, the problems pile up. When you hover a class, some of its countries may be outside the visible area, and you cannot reach them directly (unless they are neighbours) without hovering another class on the way. In this example, the tooltips cannot be hovered either.

In the end, grouping the countries works well for keyboard users: five tab stops instead of twenty-seven, and the values of the whole class shown at once. But the same choice makes the map harder to use with zoom, a screen magnifier or voice control.

In my experience, when making things better for some users makes them worse for others, it is often a sign that I need to take a step back, and that a simpler solution is worth looking for.


### Take a step back

<p class="highlight">The idea: what matters here is the groups. So the legend becomes the way in. It sits somewhere between the map and its alternative: a list of groups, linked to the visual.</p>

 <script type="module">
  // Arrow keys in the legend's country lists (a roving tabindex), as in list-keys.js, and
  // Escape to hide the shown tooltip, as in country-tooltips.js.
  // Light DOM: the content is plain HTML, which works without this script.
  customElements.define('choropleth-map', class extends HTMLElement {
    connectedCallback() {
      this.controller = new AbortController();
      const { signal } = this.controller;
      for (const list of this.querySelectorAll('.class-legend ul')) {
        const items = [...list.querySelectorAll('li')];
        const reset = () => items.forEach((item, i) => { item.tabIndex = i === 0 ? 0 : -1; });
        reset();
        list.closest('details').addEventListener('toggle', (event) => {
          if (event.newState === 'closed') reset();
        }, { signal });
        const hint = document.createElement('p');
        hint.className = 'list-hint';
        hint.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
        hint.textContent = '↑ ↓ to move through the countries';
        list.after(hint);
        list.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
          const current = items.indexOf(event.target);
          if (current === -1) return;
          const next = {
            ArrowDown: Math.min(current + 1, items.length - 1),
            ArrowUp: Math.max(current - 1, 0),
            Home: 0,
            End: items.length - 1,
          }[event.key];
          if (next === undefined) return;
          event.preventDefault(); // the arrows would scroll the page
          items[current].tabIndex = -1;
          items[next].tabIndex = 0;
          items[next].focus();
        }, { signal });
      }
      // Escape: .is-dismissed on the figure, removed when the pointer moves to another
      // country (a country and its tooltip share a code) or the focus moves.
      const figure = this.querySelector('.choropleth');
      let pointed = null;
      document.addEventListener('keydown', (event) => {
        if (event.key === 'Escape') figure.classList.add('is-dismissed');
      }, { signal });
      figure.addEventListener('pointerover', (event) => {
        const element = event.target.closest('[data-code], [data-tooltip]');
        const code = element?.dataset.code ?? element?.dataset.tooltip ?? null;
        if (code === pointed) return;
        pointed = code;
        figure.classList.remove('is-dismissed');
      }, { signal });
      figure.addEventListener('pointerleave', () => {
        pointed = null;
        figure.classList.remove('is-dismissed');
      }, { signal });
      figure.addEventListener('focusin', () => figure.classList.remove('is-dismissed'), { signal });
    }
    disconnectedCallback() {
      this.controller.abort();
    }
  });
 </script>
</choropleth-map>

Try it:

- open a class in the legend;
- move in the list with the arrow keys;
- hover a country on the map.

#### How it works

Each class of the legend is a `<details>` element: its `<summary>` gives the class and its number of countries, and its content lists the countries with their values. The `name` attribute groups them, so that opening one class closes the others.

```html
<details name="classes" data-class="20-25">
  <summary>20 to 25% <span>10 countries</span></summary>
  <ul>
    <li data-code="PL">Poland 23.7%</li>
    …
  </ul>
</details>
```

When a `<details>` is open, CSS alone dims the other classes on the map, with `:has()`:

```css
.choropleth:has(details[data-class="20-25"][open]) .tm-class:not([data-class="20-25"]) {
  opacity: .3;
}
```

The same goes for the countries: hovering a country on the map shows its value and highlights it in the open list, and hovering or focusing a country in the list outlines it on the map. As on the map of links, the tooltips can be hovered, and the <kbd>Escape</kbd> key hides them.

**Moving through the list with the arrow keys** is not standard behaviour. With the <kbd>Tab</kbd> key alone, a keyboard user would go from one `<summary>` to the next. Here, the list inside an open `<details>` is a single tab stop, and the arrow keys move from one country to the next, highlighting it on the map. This roving tabindex and the <kbd>Escape</kbd> key are the only scripts of this map.

Could this be a use case for [interactive lists](https://sarahmhigley.com/writing/interactive-lists/), as proposed by Sarah Higley?

#### What the tests say

The map itself is hidden from screen readers: all the data is in the legend. Screen reader users hear each class with its number of countries, open it, then read its countries and their values, as in any list.

Keyboard users have one tab stop per class, plus one for the open list, and see on the map where each country they reach is.

Voice control users can open a class by saying its visible name, as with any native control.

With zoom or a screen magnifier, the legend is ordinary HTML text: it grows with the zoom and, on narrow screens, sits above the map instead of beside it. The values can be read in the legend, without having to chase a tooltip across the map.

Without JavaScript, the legend still works, since `<details>` needs no script; only the arrow keys and the <kbd>Escape</kbd> key are lost.

All users can access the data. Visually impaired users should have a more comfortable experience; mouse users get the map they expect; keyboard users can move through the lists and see each country highlighted on the map. This is not a map with an alternative tacked on (a table without the groups, or a long text written as an afterthought), but an interactive legend, and I am quite satisfied with it.

## Conclusion

An SVG map can be accessible, provided it starts with the right structure. A map of links is, after all, a list of links, and SVG lets us say so with roles, names and states, just as HTML does. Things got harder when the map carried data: in my example, fixes made for one group of users tended to create new problems for another, and the design ended up arbitrating between their needs.

When that happens, it is worth taking a step back and asking what the important information really is. Here, it was the groups, not the shapes of the countries, and once the legend became the way into the data, the map could go back to what it does best: showing, at a glance, where things are. The result is simpler, and, in my tests, better for most users. I suspect this goes well beyond maps.

What do you think?
